relearning.title: Read: inclined planes
relearning.description: A short reading with the sledding-hill analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can identify and calculate the IMA, AMA, and efficiency of an inclined plane.**

**Think of climbing a sledding hill.** Charging straight up the steep side is short but exhausting. Walking up the long, gentle path takes more steps, but each step is easy. A ramp works the same way: you trade a longer distance for a smaller force.

**An inclined plane** is a flat surface that is higher on one end: wheelchair ramps, loading ramps, roads that zigzag up a hill. A **wedge** (an axe blade) and a **screw** (jar-lid threads) are modified inclined planes.

**On a ramp:** **De** = the **length** of the ramp, **Dr** = the **height**, **Fr** = the **weight** of the object, and **Fe** = the push or pull **along** the ramp.

**Formulas.** **IMA = De ÷ Dr = length ÷ height.** **AMA = Fr ÷ Fe.** IMA and AMA have no units, and a ramp's IMA is always more than 1.

**Worked example:** A wheelchair ramp is 6.4 m long and rises 0.8 m. Formula: IMA = length ÷ height. Set up: IMA = 6.4 m ÷ 0.8 m. Answer: **8** (no units). On an ideal ramp, a 560 N rider and chair would need Fe = Fr ÷ IMA = 560 N ÷ 8 = **70 N**.

checks.prompt: A ramp is 5.4 m long and 0.9 m high. What is its IMA? Type a number.
checks.explanation: IMA = length ÷ height = 5.4 m ÷ 0.9 m = 6 (no units). Dividing the height by the length (about 0.17) is the common mistake; a ramp's IMA is always more than 1.

checks.prompt: A 600 N box is pushed up a ramp with a 150 N push along the ramp. What is the AMA?
checks.explanation: AMA = Fr ÷ Fe = 600 N ÷ 150 N = 4 (no units). Flipping it (0.25) or subtracting (450) are the common mistakes.

sections.title: Work and efficiency on a ramp

body.text:
**The trade-off.** A ramp takes **less force** than lifting straight up, but you push over a **longer distance**, so it does **not** reduce the work. **Work input = Fe × De** and **Work output = Fr × Dr** (in joules). Ideal (no friction): Work in = Work out, so Fe × De = Fr × Dr.

**Efficiency = Work output ÷ Work input × 100 = AMA ÷ IMA × 100.** A real ramp is always below 100%, because friction turns some energy into heat, so the AMA is always less than the IMA. A mass in kg becomes a weight with Fr = m × 9.8.

**Worked example 2:** A student pushes a 500 N box up a ramp 3 m long and 0.6 m high with a 125 N push. Step 1: Work input = 125 N × 3 m = 375 J. Step 2: Work output = 500 N × 0.6 m = 300 J. Step 3: Efficiency = 300 J ÷ 375 J × 100 = **80%**. Other way: IMA = 3 ÷ 0.6 = 5, AMA = 500 ÷ 125 = 4, and 4 ÷ 5 × 100 = **80%**.

**Worked example 3:** A 30 kg box goes up a ramp 2.4 m long and 0.6 m high that is 70% efficient. Step 1: Fr = 30 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 294 N. Step 2: IMA = 2.4 ÷ 0.6 = 4, so the ideal Fe = 294 N ÷ 4 = 73.5 N. Step 3: The real ramp needs more: Fe = 73.5 N ÷ 0.7 = **105 N**.

**Watch out for:** dividing height ÷ length, using forces for IMA or distances for AMA, using the ramp's length for work output (output uses the height), flipping efficiency so it is over 100%, forgetting × 100, and using kg as if it were N.

checks.prompt: A 340 N box is pushed up a ramp 4 m long and 1 m high with a 100 N push. What is the efficiency? Type a number (in %).
checks.explanation: Work input = 100 N × 4 m = 400 J. Work output = 340 N × 1 m = 340 J. Efficiency = 340 J ÷ 400 J × 100 = 85%. Using the ramp's length for the output (340 N × 4 m) is the common mistake; it gives an impossible 340%.

checks.prompt: Two ramps both rise 1 m. Ramp A is 3 m long, and Ramp B is 6 m long. Which needs less effort force, and why?

options.text: Ramp A, because you push a shorter distance
Ramp B, because its IMA is 6 instead of 3
Both need the same force, because they reach the same height

checks.explanation: IMA = length ÷ height: Ramp A is 3 and Ramp B is 6. A greater IMA means less effort force, but over a longer distance. Thinking a shorter push means less force is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why a ramp lets you use less force but does not save you any work. Use the words effort force, distance, and work.

relearning.title: Do: ramp problems step by step
relearning.description: A ramp's IMA and ideal push one step at a time, then its efficiency two ways.

body.problem: A loading ramp is 4.5 m long and rises 0.9 m into a truck. A 630 N cart is pushed up it. Find the IMA and the push needed if the ramp is ideal (no friction).

steps.text: Label the ramp. De = length = 4.5 m. Dr = height = 0.9 m. Fr = the cart's weight = 630 N.
Formula: IMA = De ÷ Dr. Set up: IMA = 4.5 m ÷ 0.9 m. Answer: 5 (no units).
On an ideal ramp, AMA = IMA, so Fr ÷ Fe = 5. That means Fe = Fr ÷ IMA.
Set up: Fe = 630 N ÷ 5. Answer: 126 N. That is much less than lifting 630 N straight up, but you push 4.5 m instead of 0.9 m.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a ramp is 7.2 m long and 1.2 m high. What is its IMA? Type a number.
checks.explanation: IMA = length ÷ height = 7.2 m ÷ 1.2 m = 6 (no units). Dividing the height by the length (about 0.17) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: An ideal ramp has an IMA of 4. What push moves an 800 N crate up it?
checks.explanation: Fe = Fr ÷ IMA = 800 N ÷ 4 = 200 N. Multiplying (3,200 N) would mean the ramp makes the job harder, and subtracting (796 N) isn't how IMA works. Those are the common mistakes.

body.problem: A student pushes a 450 N cart up a ramp 4 m long and 0.8 m high with a 120 N push along the ramp. Find the efficiency using work, then check it with AMA ÷ IMA.

steps.text: Work input uses the effort: Work input = Fe × De = 120 N × 4 m = 480 J.
Work output uses the load and the height: Work output = Fr × Dr = 450 N × 0.8 m = 360 J.
Formula: Efficiency = Work output ÷ Work input × 100. Set up: 360 J ÷ 480 J × 100. Answer: 75%.
Check it the other way. IMA = 4 m ÷ 0.8 m = 5. AMA = 450 N ÷ 120 N = 3.75. Efficiency = 3.75 ÷ 5 × 100 = 75%. Same answer.

checks.prompt: A 300 N box is pushed up a ramp 2.5 m long onto a stage 0.6 m high. What is the work output?
checks.explanation: Work output = Fr × Dr = 300 N × 0.6 m = 180 J: the weight times the height. Using the ramp's length (300 N × 2.5 m = 750 J) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a ramp has an IMA of 6 and an AMA of 4.8. What is its efficiency? Type a number (in %).
checks.explanation: Efficiency = AMA ÷ IMA × 100 = 4.8 ÷ 6 × 100 = 80%. Flipping it (125%) is the common mistake; a real ramp is always below 100%.

sections.title: Inclined plane explained: IMA, AMA and efficiency

checks.prompt: A ramp is 5 m long and 1 m high. What is its IMA? Type a number.
checks.explanation: IMA = length ÷ height = 5 m ÷ 1 m = 5 (no units). Dividing height ÷ length (0.2) is the common mistake; a ramp's IMA is always more than 1.

checks.prompt: A student pushes a 400 N box up a ramp with an IMA of 5 using a 100 N push. What is the ramp's efficiency?
checks.explanation: AMA = Fr ÷ Fe = 400 N ÷ 100 N = 4. Efficiency = AMA ÷ IMA × 100 = 4 ÷ 5 × 100 = 80%. Flipping it (125%) is the common mistake; a real ramp is always below 100%.

sections.title: Mechanical advantage of an inclined plane

checks.prompt: Compared with lifting a box straight up onto a stage, pushing it up an ideal ramp takes...

options.text: less force over a longer distance, and the same work
less force over a longer distance, and less work
more force over a shorter distance

checks.explanation: A ramp trades a longer distance for a smaller force. It does not reduce the work: on an ideal ramp, Fe × De = Fr × Dr. Thinking a ramp saves work is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A loading ramp must reach a truck bed 1 m high. Which change makes the ramp's IMA bigger?

options.text: Make the ramp shorter and steeper

checks.explanation: IMA = length ÷ height. The height stays 1 m, so a longer ramp gives a bigger IMA and an easier push. A shorter, steeper ramp lowers the IMA.

sections.shortAnswer: A wheelchair ramp is being built up to a door 0.5 m off the ground. Explain why a longer ramp is easier to push a chair up, using IMA = length ÷ height.
